The subject/object relationship is reversed: in Hebrew, God is the one who has not cursed (the object of the curse is the people), and Balaam cannot curse them. In Vietnamese, it implies God causes Balaam to curse, which is the opposite. Similarly, the second line: 'וּמָה אֶזְעֹם לֹא זָעַם יְהוָה' means 'How can I denounce whom Yahweh has not denounced?' but the Vietnamese says 'Đức Giê-hô-va nào khiến ta nổi giận, thì ta không thể nổi giận' meaning 'If Yahweh causes me to be angry, I cannot be angry' — again reversing the subject/object and changing the claim.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'נְאֻם בִּלְעָם' means 'the oracle/utterance of Balaam', not 'Đức Giê-hô-va phán vậy' (Thus says Yahweh). omission: The Hebrew says 'Phinehas son of Eleazar son of Aaron the priest' (פִּֽינְחָ֨ס בֶּן אֶלְעָזָ֜ר בֶּן אַהֲרֹ֣ן הַכֹּהֵ֗ן), but the Vietnamese omits 'son of Eleazar' (bèn E-lê-a-sa), only saying 'con trai A-rôn' (son of Aaron).

name_swap: The Hebrew has כָּזְבִּי (Kozbi), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'Cốt-bi' — the name is not a standard transliteration of Kozbi; it appears to be a different name (possibly a typo or substitution).
name_swap: The Hebrew says 'Eleazar son of Aaron the priest' (אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן אַהֲרֹן), but the Vietnamese says 'A-rôn' (Aaron), omitting Eleazar and substituting Aaron in his place.
mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'sáu mươi bảy ngàn năm trăm' (67,500), but the Vietnamese says 'sáu mươi ngàn bảy trăm năm mươi' (60,750). The number is wrong: the Hebrew has 67,500, not 60,750.
mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'fifty-two thousand seven hundred' (52,700), but the Vietnamese says 'hai mươi lăm ngàn bảy trăm' (25,700). The number is wrong.

mistranslation: The Hebrew number is 'sáu trăm ngàn và một ngàn bảy trăm ba mươi' (601,730). The Vietnamese renders it as 'sáu trăm một ngàn bảy trăm ba mươi' (601,730? addition: The Vietnamese adds 'Y-sơ-ra-ên' (Israel) as the subject, which is not present in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew says 'they will inherit' (יִנְחָלוּ) with the implied subject being the tribes, not explicitly 'Israel'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew word 'עִשָּׂרוֹן' (issaron) means 'tenth part' (of an ephah, a dry measure), not 'ếch' (frog). The Vietnamese rendering 'một phần mười ếch' introduces an animal (frog) that is not in the Hebrew, changing the meaning entirely. The correct translation should be 'một phần mười ê-pha' or 'một phần mười' (a tenth of an ephah).
mistranslation: Hebrew says 'mười một' (11) con bò đực (עַשְׁתֵּי עָשָׂר), but Vietnamese says 'mười hai' (12).

omission: The Hebrew list includes 'və'el'aleh' (וְאֶלְעָלֵה), meaning 'and Elealeh', which is missing from the Vietnamese translation. The Vietnamese lists A-ta-rốt, Đi-bôn, Gia-ê-xe, Nim-ra, Hết-bôn, Sê-bam, Nê-bô, and Bê-ôn, but omits Elealeh entirely.

omission: The Hebrew phrase 'מֽוּסַבֹּ֥ת שֵׁ֖ם' (whose name was changed) is not fully rendered; the Vietnamese says 'rồi đổi tên Síp-ma' (then changed the name of Sibmah), but the Hebrew indicates that Nebo and Baal-meon had their names changed, and Sibmah is listed as a third city, not the object of the renaming. The Vietnamese omits the renaming of Nebo and Baal-meon and incorrectly attaches the renaming to Sibmah.
name_swap: Place name 'עֶצְיוֹן גָּבֶר' (Ezion-geber) is rendered as 'Ghê-be', dropping 'Ezion' and only keeping 'Geber'.
name_swap: Hebrew 'עִיִּים' (Iyyim) is rendered as 'Y-giê-A-ba-rim' (Iye-abarim), which is a different place name. The Hebrew text has only 'Iyyim', not 'Iye-abarim'.

name_swap: The Hebrew lists the daughters as Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah. The Vietnamese renders 'Thiệt-sa' for Tirzah and 'Minh-ca' for Milcah, but 'Hốt-la' for Hoglah is correct. The issue is that 'Minh-ca' appears to be a swapped or altered name for Milcah (מִלְכָּה), which should be 'Min-ca' or similar, not 'Minh-ca' — though this may be a transliteration variant. The main flag is that 'Minh-ca' for Milcah is a minor transliteration difference, not a substantive error. Re-evaluating: the names are all present and in order; the transliterations are acceptable. The real issue is that the Vietnamese says 'các con trai của cậu mình' (sons of their uncle) which matches 'sons of their uncles' (לִבְנֵי דֹדֵיהֶן) — this is correct. The verb 'đều trở thành vợ' (became wives) matches 'were for wives' (לְנָשִׁים). No omission or addition. The only possible flag is the name 'Minh-ca' vs 'Milcah' — but this is a transliteration choice, not a name swap. Therefore, verdict should be OK.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'in the fortieth year' (בְּאַרְבָּעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה), but the Vietnamese says 'Năm mươi ngày bốn mươi' which is nonsensical ('fifty days forty') and does not convey 'fortieth year'.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'לָבַז יִהְיֶה' means 'will be for plunder' (i.e., will be plundered/spoiled), but Vietnamese renders it as 'sẽ bị tiêu diệt' ('will be destroyed'), which changes the meaning from plunder to destruction.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'the land of Og king of Bashan' (וְאֶת אֶרֶץ עוֹג מֶלֶךְ הַבָּשָׁן), but the Vietnamese renders 'đất Ba-san, tức là vua Oùc' ('the land of Bashan, that is, King Og'), which reverses the relationship: it identifies Bashan as Og rather than Og as king of Bashan. However, the Hebrew does not mention 'from Aroer' (מֵאֲרוֹעֵר) in this verse; the Vietnamese adds 'từ A-rô-e' ('from Aroer'), which is an addition not present in the Hebrew text.

name_swap: The Hebrew has 'núi Si-ôn' (הַר שִׂיאֹן, Mount Sion), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'núi Si-ri-ôn' (Mount Sirion), which is a different name (שִׂרְיֹן, Sirion, cf. Deut 3:9). This swaps the mountain name.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'zovechei ha-zevach' means 'those who slaughter/sacrifice the sacrifice' (a peace/fellowship offering, zebach), not 'dâng của lễ thiêu' (burnt offering, olah). The Hebrew term 'zebach' specifically refers to a peace/sacrificial offering, not a burnt offering. This changes the type of offering described.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'נִשְׁבַּע' means 'swore' (made an oath), but Vietnamese renders it as 'đã chỉ' (has shown/pointed out), which changes the meaning from an oath to a demonstration.

addition: The Vietnamese adds 'Nếu người trai trẻ ấy không bị ném đá' (If that young man is not stoned), a conditional clause not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew begins directly with 'And they shall bring out the young woman...' (וְהוֹצִיאוּ אֶת הנער), with no such condition.

addition: The Vietnamese adds 'ngươi phải dùng nó đào hố, rồi lấp lại phân của mình' (you must use it to dig a hole, then cover your excrement), which is not present in the Hebrew verse. The Hebrew only says 'you shall have a peg outside the camp, and you shall go out there outside' — the digging and covering instructions appear in the following verse (Deut 23:13), not here.
mistranslation: The Hebrew word 'יָתֵד' means 'peg' or 'stake', not 'cây chổi' (broom). This changes the object being described.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'לֹא תִמְצָא חֵן בְּעֵינָיו' means 'she does not find favor in his eyes' (i.e., in the husband's eyes), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'nàng không đẹp lòng người trước mặt Đức Giê-hô-va' ('she does not please him before the LORD'), incorrectly adding 'trước mặt Đức Giê-hô-va' (before the LORD) which is not in the Hebrew text and changes the meaning by implying the displeasure is before God rather than in the husband's eyes.

number_person_tense: The Hebrew second-person singular verbs וְהִנַּחְתּוֹ ('you will set it') and וְהִשְׁתַּחֲוִיתָ ('you will worship') are addressed to the individual worshiper (singular 'you'), but the Vietnamese renders them as 'tôi sẽ đặt' (I will set) and 'anh em sẽ thờ lạy' (you all will worship), changing the person and number. The first verb is wrongly shifted to first person, and the second to plural second person, altering who performs the actions.

name_swap: The Hebrew says 'Đức Giê-hô-va' (YHWH) swore to your fathers, but the Vietnamese adds 'Đức Chúa Trời' (God) as the object of the oath, making it 'swore by God' instead of 'swore to your fathers'. This changes the meaning: the Hebrew has YHWH swearing to the fathers, not swearing by God.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וּלְחֻמֵי רֶשֶׁף' means 'consumed by plague/burning' (literally 'eaten by Resheph'), but Vietnamese renders 'bị thiêu đốt bởi cơn giận dữ' ('burned by wrath/anger'), introducing 'cơn giận dữ' (wrath) which is not in the Hebrew; 'רֶשֶׁף' is a noun meaning 'flame/plague' (often a deity of plague), not 'anger'.

omission: The Hebrew opening לוּלֵי כַּעַס אוֹיֵב אָגוּר ('Were it not that I feared the provocation of the enemy') is entirely missing; the Vietnamese begins with 'Chớ sợ kẻ thù oán sẽ nhạo báng' ('Do not fear the enemy's resentment will mock'), which changes the meaning from a hypothetical 'if not for' statement to a command not to fear, and also omits the concept of 'provocation/anger' (כַּעַס) and 'I feared' (אָגוּר).; mistranslation: The Hebrew פֶּן יְנַכְּרוּ צָרֵימוֹ means 'lest their adversaries misunderstand/misjudge' (i.e., the enemies of Israel misinterpreting God's action), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'e kẻ địch mình hiểu lầm' ('lest our enemies misunderstand'), which is close but the subject 'their adversaries' (צָרֵימוֹ) is rendered as 'our enemies' (kẻ địch mình), shifting the referent from the enemies of the people (Israel's foes) to a generic 'our enemies'—this is a minor shift but still changes who is being referred to.; addition: The Vietnamese adds 'sẽ nhạo báng' ('will mock') which has no direct Hebrew equivalent; the Hebrew has 'provocation of the enemy' (כַּעַס אוֹיֵב) and 'lest they say' (פֶּן יֹאמְרוּ), but no explicit 'mock' verb. This addition introduces a concept not present in the Hebrew.

addition: The Hebrew text does not name the subject as 'Đức Giê-hô-va' (Yahweh); it simply says 'he became king' (וַיְהִ֥י בִישֻׁר֖וּן מֶ֑לֶךְ). The subject is implied from context, but the Vietnamese explicitly adds 'Đức Giê-hô-va', which is an addition not present in the Hebrew clause.

mistranslation: Câu tiếng Việt thiếu đại từ 'người' (him) trong cụm 'đã tranh luận với tại các nước Mê-ri-ba' — nguyên văn Hebrew 'תְּרִיבֵהוּ' có hậu tố 'הוּ' (him), nên phải là 'đã tranh luận với người ấy tại các nước Mê-ri-ba'.

addition: The Hebrew text does not mention 'Đức Chúa Trời' (God) as the subject of the burial; the subject is implicit (Moses, from context), and the verb is simply 'he buried him.' Adding 'God' introduces a subject not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'Joshua said to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh' (יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אָמַר לֵאמֹר). The Vietnamese renders it as 'The LORD spoke to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh through Joshua' (Đức Giê-hô-va nói ... qua Giô-suê), which reverses the subject and object: it makes the LORD the speaker and Joshua the mediator, whereas the Hebrew has Joshua as the speaker addressing the tribes. This changes who is doing what to whom.
name_swap: The Hebrew place name is גִּלְגָּל (Gilgal), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'Gi-ê-lê-ga', which is a different name and not a recognized transliteration of Gilgal.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מֵעֲבוּר הָאָרֶץ' means 'from the produce of the land' (i.e., the yield/crops of the land), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'các sản phẩm từ mùa gặt đầu tiên của đất' ('products from the first harvest of the land'), adding 'đầu tiên' (first) which is not in the Hebrew and changes the meaning to imply a specific first harvest.

addition: The Hebrew text says 'they were struck/smitten' (וַיִּנָּֽגְע֛וּ), meaning they were defeated/struck down, but the Vietnamese adds 'giả vờ thua trận' (pretended to lose the battle), which is an addition not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew simply states they were struck before them, not that they feigned defeat.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'נִמְצְאוּ' means 'were found', not 'đã bị bắt' (were captured). The Vietnamese adds the concept of capture which is not in the Hebrew; the kings were found hiding, not captured at this point.
name_swap: The Hebrew place name is לָכִישָׁה (Lachish), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'Ha-kích', which is a different name. It should be 'La-ki-sơ' or similar.

name_swap: The Hebrew place name is עֶגְלֹנָה (Eglon), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'Ê-đa-ron', which is a different name (likely a confusion with Adullam or another site). The correct transliteration should be 'Ê-glôn' or similar.

name_swap: Hebrew has 'עַד עַזָּה' (as far as Gaza), but Vietnamese renders 'cho đến Ách-cáp' (as far as Achzib/Achshaph), swapping Gaza for a different place name.; addition: Vietnamese adds 'Bết Nê-ên' (Beth Neein/Beth Nehel) which is not present in the Hebrew text; the Hebrew only mentions Kadesh-barnea, Gaza, Goshen, and Gibeon.

addition: The Vietnamese adds 'Đức Giê-hô-va phán cùng Giô-suê, người bèn' ('The LORD spoke to Joshua, and he then...') which has no basis in the Hebrew text. name_swap: Hebrew has 'עֶגְלוֹן' (Eglon) and 'גֶּזֶר' (Gezer). Vietnamese renders 'Ê-đôn' (Edom) and 'Kê-xe' (likely a misreading of Gezer as 'Kê-xe' — but the first name is clearly wrong: Eglon is not Edom).

name_swap: Hebrew has 'vua của Si-mê-rôn Mê-rôn' (מֶלֶךְ שִׁמְרוֹן מְראוֹן), but Vietnamese renders it as 'vua của Si-chem' (Shechem), which is a different place name. The Hebrew name is Shimron-meron, not Shechem.
name_swap: Hebrew 'יָקְנֳעָם' (Jokneam) is rendered as 'Giô-ke-than' (Joktheel), a different place name. The correct Vietnamese transliteration should be 'Giô-kê-nê-am' or similar.

name_swap: The Hebrew lists the five Philistine lords as: Gaza (הָעַזָּתִי), Ashdod (הָאַשְׁדּוֹדִי), Ashkelon (הָאֶשְׁקְלוֹנִי), Gath (הַגִּתִּי), and Ekron (הָעֶקְרוֹנִי). The first item 'người Gát' is wrong—it should be 'người Ga-xa' (Gaza). The fourth item 'người Gít' appears to be a mistranslation of 'Gittite' (Gath) again, but the Hebrew has 'הַגִּתִּי' (Gath) as the fourth, so the order is swapped: the first should be Gaza, and the fourth should be Gath. The Vietnamese has Gath first and then a second Gath-like name 'Gít' for the fourth, omitting Gaza entirely and duplicating Gath.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'the great man among the Anakim' (הָאָדָם הַגָּדוֹל בָּעֲנָקִים), referring to Arba as a great/important man among the Anakim, not 'a person of advanced age' (một người lớn tuổi). The Vietnamese rendering 'lớn tuổi' (old/elderly) changes the meaning from 'great/important' to 'old in age'.

name_swap: The Hebrew says Othniel (עָתְנִיאֵל) son of Kenaz, but the Vietnamese renders the name as 'Kên-đát' (Caleb's son? Actually Kên-đát is not Othniel; it appears to be a different name, possibly a confusion with 'Caleb' or another name). The correct name should be 'Ốt-ni-ên' or similar, not 'Kên-đát'.

name_swap: Hebrew 'חֲדָשָׁה' (Hadashah) is rendered 'Ha-đa-sa' (missing the final 'h' sound, but more importantly the Hebrew has 'חֲדָשָׁה' not 'חֲדָשָׁ' – the Vietnamese 'Ha-đa-sa' drops the final 'h' which is part of the name; however, the more significant issue is that 'מִגְדַּל גָּד' (Migdal-gad) is rendered 'Mích-đanh Gad' – 'Mích-đanh' is not a transliteration of 'מִגְדַּל' (Migdal) but appears to be a different name (possibly 'Migdol' or a corruption), and the Hebrew has 'גָּד' (Gad) which is correctly 'Gad', but the first part is wrong. The correct transliteration should be 'Mích-đan Gát' or similar. The name 'Mích-đanh' is a mistranslation/name swap for 'Migdal'.
name_swap: The Hebrew place name עֶגְלוֹן (Eglon) is rendered as 'Ê-đôn' (Edom), which is a different name. The correct Vietnamese transliteration should be 'Ét-lôn' or similar, not 'Ê-đôn'.

name_swap: The Hebrew place name 'שׂוֹכֹה' (Sokoh) is rendered as 'Xô-cô' which is acceptable, but 'שָׁמִיר' (Shamir) is rendered as 'Sâm-ia' — this appears to be a corruption or misreading; the correct transliteration should be 'Sa-mia' or 'Samia' (not 'Sâm-ia'), and 'יַתִּיר' (Jattir) is rendered as 'Gia-tia' — the Hebrew has 'יַתִּיר' (Yattir), not 'Gia-tia' (which would be 'יַתִּיר' with a gimel, but the Hebrew has yod). The name 'Gia-tia' is a mistransliteration of 'Jattir' (יַתִּיר), which should be 'Gia-tia' is not standard; the correct is 'Gia-tia' is not the Hebrew, but the Hebrew is 'יַתִּיר' (Yattir) — the Vietnamese 'Gia-tia' introduces a 'G' sound not in the Hebrew, and 'Sâm-ia' for 'שָׁמִיר' (Shamir) is a misreading (the Hebrew has 'shin-mem-yod-resh', not 'shin-ayin-mem-yod-ayin'). These are name swaps/mistransliterations that would mislead a reader.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הֶאָמַר נָשָׂאתִי' means 'I have borne/uttered a saying' (i.e., 'I have spoken'), not 'I have sinned' (phạm tội). The Vietnamese adds 'Tôi đã phạm tội' which is not in the Hebrew and changes the meaning. The Hebrew clause 'לֹא אֶחְבֹּל' means 'I will not transgress/act corruptly' (or 'I will not pledge/endanger'), not 'I will no longer be wicked' (tôi sẽ không còn gian ác nữa) — the Vietnamese adds 'còn... nữa' implying a past state of wickedness that is not stated in the Hebrew.
name_swap: The Hebrew has 'Iyyov' (Gióp), but the Vietnamese renders 'Ích-tháp' (Ishbak?), a different name.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'בְּשֶׁלַח' means 'by the sword' (instrumental 'by'), but Vietnamese renders 'vì gươm dao' ('because of the sword'), shifting the sense from instrument to cause. This is a minor semantic shift but changes the claim from 'they will pass through by the sword' to 'they will die because of the sword'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וַיְצַו עָלֶיהָ בְמַפְגִּיעַ' means 'and commands it (the light) by/against the storm/cloud' (the noun מַפְגִּיעַ is a hapax, often rendered 'storm' or 'cloud' in context of Job 36:32). The Vietnamese 'truyền cho nó phải đánh vào nơi nào' ('commands it to strike at some place') adds the idea of striking a place, which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew says he commands it (the light) by means of a storm/cloud, not that it strikes a place. This changes the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מִקְנֶה אַף עַל עוֹלֶה' is rendered as 'còn súc vật thì cảm thấy cơn bão sắp tới' (but the animals feel the coming storm). The Hebrew phrase literally means 'even the cattle (or possessions) upon the burnt offering' or 'even the cattle on the ascent' (referring to the burnt offering ascending). The Vietnamese adds 'cảm thấy cơn bão sắp tới' (feel the coming storm) which is not in the Hebrew and changes the meaning. The Hebrew is about the friend declaring/proclaiming about him (Job), and the cattle even upon the burnt offering (i.e., even the cattle used for the burnt offering are affected). The Vietnamese introduces a storm concept not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְלֹא יְעַקְּבֵם' means 'and He does not restrain them' (referring to the thunder/lightnings), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'chẳng ai cản được ánh chớp' ('no one can stop the lightning'), which changes the subject from God to 'no one' and adds 'ánh chớp' (lightning) not present in the Hebrew.

addition: The Hebrew 'הוּא בַּשְּׁחָקִים' means 'He is in the skies/clouds' (referring to God), but the Vietnamese adds 'vì Ngài đã ẩn mình' ('because He has hidden Himself'), introducing the concept of hiding that is not in the Hebrew text.

name_swap: The Hebrew 'עַיִשׁ' (Ayish, likely the constellation Ursa Major/Big Dipper) is rendered as 'sao Mai' (the Morning Star/Venus), which is a different celestial object. The Hebrew also has 'עַל בָּנֶיהָ' ('with its sons/children'), which the Vietnamese renders as 'cùng các con của nó' (with its children), but the name swap changes the referent.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'רְנָנִים' (renanim) is often understood as 'ostrich' (or a bird of joy), not 'chim công' (peacock). The second clause 'אִם אֶבְרָה חֲסִידָה וְנֹצָה' literally means 'if (it has) wing of stork and plumage' — the Hebrew is a conditional/assertion about the ostrich having stork-like wings and feathers, not a rhetorical question about 'lòng nhân từ' (kindness/mercy). The Vietnamese adds 'há có lòng nhân từ chăng?' (does it have kindness?) which is not in the Hebrew and changes the meaning entirely.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בְּרַעַשׁ וְרֹגֶז יְגַמֶּא אָרֶץ' means 'He swallows the ground with fierceness and rage' (the horse swallows/dashes the ground). The Vietnamese 'Nó hí vang, ngậm đất, rung chuyển cả đất đai' adds 'hí vang' (neighs loudly) which is not in the Hebrew, and 'rung chuyển cả đất đai' (shakes the whole land) is an addition; the Hebrew only says 'swallows the ground' with 'ra'ash and rogez' (trembling and rage) as manner, not that the land trembles. This changes the imagery and adds concepts not present.

mistranslation: The Hebrew has 'הֲרֹב עִם שַׁדַּי יִסּוֹר' ('Will the one who contends with Shaddai be corrected/chastened?') — the subject is a third-person 'he who contends', not 'you'. The Vietnamese renders it as 'Đức Chúa Trời Toàn Năng há sẽ tranh luận cùng ngươi sao?' ('Will God Almighty argue with you?'), reversing the subject and object: in Hebrew, the human contends with God, not God with the human. This changes who is doing what to whom.; mistranslation: The second clause 'מוֹכִיחַ אֱלוֹהַּ יַעֲנֶנָּה' means 'the one who reproves God, let him answer it' (i.e., the human reproves God and must answer). The Vietnamese 'Đấng Toàn Năng há sẽ đáp lại ngươi khi ngươi bắt bẻ Ngài?' ('Will the Almighty answer you when you reprove Him?') again reverses the roles: in Hebrew the human reproves God and is challenged to answer; in Vietnamese God answers the human. mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בְשֻׂכּוֹת' (with thorns/hooks) is rendered as 'lưới' (net), and 'בְצִלְצַל' (with a fish spear/harpoon) is rendered as 'ngọn giáo câu cá' (fishing spear). The first term 'שֻׂכּוֹת' specifically means 'thorns' or 'barbs', not 'net'. This changes the imagery from filling the skin with thorns/hooks to filling it with a net, which is a substantive difference in the verse's claim.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הֲגַם אֶל מַרְאָיו יֻטָֽל' is a rhetorical question: 'Is he not cast down at the sight of him?' (i.e., even at the sight of him, is one not thrown down/overwhelmed?). The Vietnamese renders it as 'còn chi thấy hình dạng nó mà không kinh hãi sao?' meaning 'and who seeing its form would not be terrified?' This changes the subject: the Hebrew says the creature (Leviathan) is cast down at the sight of it (i.e., people are overwhelmed), but the Vietnamese makes it about the viewer's fear, not the creature being cast down. The verb 'יֻטָֽל' (is thrown/cast down) is not rendered; instead an added concept of 'kinh hãi' (terrified) is introduced, and the passive sense of the creature being cast down is lost.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לֹֽא אַ֭כְזָר כִּ֣י יְעוּרֶ֑נּוּ' means 'No one is so fierce that he dares to rouse him' (i.e., no one is bold/fierce enough to stir him up). The Vietnamese 'Chẳng ai dám trêu chọc nó khi nó đang nổi giận' adds 'khi nó đang nổi giận' (when it is angry), which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew does not specify 'when angry' but rather 'no one is fierce enough to rouse him.' This addition changes the nuance of the claim.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הֶעָשׂוּ לִבְלִי חָת' means 'made without fear' (i.e., created to be fearless), but the Vietnamese 'mọi vật cao trọng đều bị nó coi thường' means 'all lofty things are despised by it', which adds the concept of despising/contempt not present in the Hebrew and changes the meaning.

addition: The Vietnamese adds 'Đức Chúa Trời ơi' (O God) at the beginning, which is not present in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew begins with 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ לְדָוִד' (For the choir director, of David), which is omitted entirely in the Vietnamese rendering.; omission: The Hebrew superscription 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ לְדָוִד' (For the choir director, of David) is missing from the Vietnamese translation.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עֲצַת עָנִי תָבִישׁוּ' means 'You (plural) put to shame the counsel of the poor/afflicted' — the subject is the wicked (implied from context, but the verb is second-person plural 'you shame'), and the object is 'the counsel of the poor'. The Vietnamese renders it as 'Kẻ ác làm bại mưu người khốn cùng' ('The wicked frustrate the plan of the poor'), changing the subject from 'you' (the wicked addressed) to 'the wicked' as a third-person agent, and shifting 'counsel/advice' (עֵצָה) to 'mưu' (scheme/plot), which alters the meaning. The Hebrew does not say 'the wicked' here; it addresses the wicked directly as 'you'.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'בְלִיַּעַל' (belial) means 'worthlessness' or 'wickedness', not 'Phán Xét' (Judgment). The phrase 'נַחֲלֵי בְלִיַּעַל' is 'torrents of destruction/wickedness', not 'dòng nước của Phán Xét'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי' means 'for You are with me' (second person, addressing God). The Vietnamese renders it as 'vì Đức Giê-hô-va ở cùng tôi' ('for Jehovah is with me'), changing the second-person address to a third-person reference to God. This alters the person and the direct address of the verse.
name_swap: The Hebrew has 'אַתָּה' (You) referring to God, but the Vietnamese renders it as 'Đức Giê-hô-va' (the LORD) twice, which is an addition/name swap not present in the Hebrew text.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'בְאָהֳלוֹ' means 'in His tent' (referring to YHWH's tent), but Vietnamese renders 'trong đền Ngài' ('in His temple'), changing the location from a tent to a temple.

omission: The Hebrew text is a conditional sentence: 'If I had not believed to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living...' (with the implied consequence 'I would have fainted/despaired'). The Vietnamese adds an explicit consequence clause 'thì tôi đã thất vọng rồi' (then I would have despaired) which is not present in the Hebrew text. While this is a common interpretive completion, it is an addition of a clause not in the Hebrew, changing the verse from an incomplete conditional (implying the result) to a fully stated one. However, the Hebrew does imply the consequence, so this is arguably acceptable. The more significant issue is the rendering of 'בְּֽטוּב יְהוָה' as 'sự tốt lành của Đức Giê-hô-va' (the goodness of the LORD) which is correct, and 'בְּאֶרֶץ חַיִּים' as 'tại đất người sống' (in the land of the living) which is correct. The main problem is the added consequence clause, which is not in the Hebrew but is a natural completion. Since the instruction says to flag only if the Vietnamese reader would come away believing something factually different or missing something substantive, the added clause does not change the meaning but adds an explicit result. This is borderline; however, the Hebrew text is a protasis without an apodosis, and the Vietnamese supplies the apodosis, which is a substantive addition. I will flag it as an addition.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'חַסְדּוֹ' means 'His lovingkindness/mercy' (God's), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'sự nhân từ của tôi' ('my lovingkindness'), changing the possessor from God to the speaker.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לִמְצֹא עֲוֺנוֹ לִשְׂנֹא' means 'to find his iniquity to hate [it]' (i.e., to discover his own sin so as to hate it), but the Vietnamese 'để không thấy tội mình mà ghét bỏ' adds 'không' (not), reversing the meaning to 'so as not to see his sin and hate it'.

addition: The Vietnamese adds 'Đức Giê-hô-va phán:' ('The LORD says:') at the beginning, which has no basis in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew begins directly with 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ' (For the choir director) and then 'אָמַרְתִּי' ('I said'), with no divine speech introduction.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לִרְקָמוֹת' (with embroidered things/garments) is an adverbial phrase describing how the virgin is brought to the king ('in embroidered work'), but the Vietnamese renders it as a separate clause 'nàng được mang đến cùng các hoa văn thêu tay' (she is brought with embroidered patterns), which changes the meaning: the Hebrew says she is brought to the king in embroidered garments, not that she is brought along with embroidered patterns as a separate item. This alters the sense of the verse.

addition: The Vietnamese adds 'Đức Giê-hô-va phán' (The LORD says), which has no basis in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew begins with 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ לִבְנֵי קֹרַח מִזְמוֹר' (For the choir director, for the sons of Korah, a psalm), then 'שִׁמְעוּ זֹאת כָּל הָעַמִּים' (Hear this, all peoples). The phrase 'Đức Giê-hô-va phán' is an addition not present in the Hebrew and changes the verse's claim by attributing the speech to the LORD.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עֲוֹן עֲקֵבַי' means 'the iniquity of my heels/supplanters' (i.e., the iniquity that dogs my steps, or the iniquity of those who follow me), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'tội ác của những kẻ theo sau tôi' (the crimes of those who follow me), which shifts the meaning from 'my own iniquity' (or 'the iniquity at my heels') to 'the crimes of others.' This changes the subject of the clause: in Hebrew, the speaker's own iniquity surrounds him, but in Vietnamese, it is the crimes of others that surround him.

addition: The Hebrew 'וְזִ֥יז שָׂ֝דַ֗י' refers to 'the creeping/teeming things of the field' (or 'the moving things of the field'), not 'mọi loài vật chạy nhảy trong đồng cỏ' (all animals running/leaping in the meadow). The Vietnamese adds 'chạy nhảy' (running/leaping) which is not in the Hebrew, and 'đồng cỏ' (meadow) is a specific rendering of 'field' that may be acceptable, but the main issue is the added descriptor 'chạy nhảy' which is not present in the Hebrew.

omission: The Hebrew superscription 'בְּבוֹא אֵלָיו נָתָן הַנָּבִיא כַּאֲשֶׁר בָּא אֶל בַּת שָׁבַע' (When Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba) is entirely omitted from the Vietnamese translation.

addition: The Hebrew text does not mention 'Đức Giê-hô-va' (the LORD/Yahweh); it simply says 'you have crushed' (דִּכִּיתָ) with the subject being God implied from context, but the divine name is not present in this verse. Adding 'Đức Giê-hô-va' introduces a name not in the Hebrew.

addition: The Hebrew begins with 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ מַשְׂכִּיל לְדָוִד' (For the chief musician, a contemplation of David), which is entirely omitted in the Vietnamese. The Vietnamese adds 'Đức Chúa Trời ơi' (O God) as a vocative, which is not present in the Hebrew text (the Hebrew has no address to God in this verse).

omission: The Hebrew opening clause 'בְּבוֹא דּוֹאֵג הָאֲדֹמִי וַיַּגֵּד לְשָׁאוּל וַיֹּאמֶר לוֹ בָּא דָוִד אֶל בֵּית אֲחִימֶלֶךְ' (When Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, saying to him, 'David came to the house of Ahimelech') is entirely omitted from the Vietnamese translation. The Vietnamese begins directly with 'Lưỡi ngươi toan bày điều ác' (Your tongue plots evil), which corresponds to the second half of the verse, leaving out the historical reference to Doeg, Saul, and Ahimelech.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַוּוֹת תַּחְשֹׁב לְשׁוֹנֶךָ' (Your tongue plots destruction/evil) is rendered as 'Lưỡi ngươi toan bày điều ác' (Your tongue plots evil), which is acceptable, but the phrase 'כְּתַעַר מְלֻטָּשׁ עֹשֵׂה רְמִיָּה' (like a sharp razor, working deceit) is rendered as 'lưỡi ngươi làm điều giả dối như dao cạo bén' (your tongue does deceit like a sharp razor), which is close. However, the omission of the entire first half of the verse (the historical context) is a substantive omission that changes the reader's understanding of the psalm's setting.

addition: The Hebrew text does not contain 'Đức Giê-hô-va phán' (The LORD says/speaks). This is an added clause not present in the Hebrew, which introduces a speaker not in the original text.; omission: The Hebrew phrase 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ אַל תַּשְׁחֵת' (For the chief musician, 'Do not destroy') is entirely omitted in the Vietnamese translation. This is a substantive omission of the psalm's title/superscription.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַֽאֻמְנָ֗ם אֵ֣לֶם צֶ֭דֶק תְּדַבֵּר֑וּן' is a rhetorical question: 'Do you indeed speak righteousness, O mute ones?' The Vietnamese renders it as a statement 'các ngươi thật sự không nói lời công bình' (you truly do not speak righteous words), which changes the interrogative into an assertion and adds 'không' (not), reversing the meaning.; addition: The phrase 'lòng các ngươi làm điều bất chính' (your hearts do injustice) has no basis in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew has 'מֵישָׁרִים תִּשְׁפְּטוּ בְּנֵי אָדָם' (you judge uprightly the sons of men), which is a separate clause, not a statement about hearts doing injustice.

omission: The Vietnamese translation omits the entire first half of the Hebrew verse (בְּהַצּוֹת֨וֹ אֶ֥ת אֲרַ֣ם נַהֲרַיִם֮ וְאֶת אֲרַ֪ם צ֫וֹבָ֥ה וַיָּ֤שָׁב יוֹאָ֗ב וַיַּ֣ךְ אֶת אֱד֣וֹם בְּגֵיא מֶ֑לַח שְׁנֵ֖ים עָשָׂ֣ר אָֽלֶף), which describes David's conflict with Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah, Joab's return and striking Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand. The Vietnamese text only renders the second half (the psalm-like cry about the earth trembling and being healed), leaving out the historical narrative entirely.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מִפְּנֵי קֹשֶׁט' means 'from before the bow' (i.e., from the face of the bow/archery), referring to protection from the enemy's bow. The Vietnamese renders it as 'vì lẽ thật' ('because of the truth'), which is a mistranslation—'קֹשֶׁט' (qoshet) means 'bow' (weapon), not 'truth' (which would be 'אֱמֶת'). This changes the meaning of the verse.

name_swap: The Hebrew text addresses 'Elohim' (אֱלֹהִים), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'Đức Giê-hô-va' (Yahweh/Jehovah), swapping the divine name.; omission: The Hebrew superscription 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ עַל נְגִינַת לְדָוִד' (For the leader, on stringed instruments, of David) is entirely omitted in the Vietnamese.
addition: The Hebrew text ends with 'Selah' (סֶלָה), but the Vietnamese adds 'ngự nơi cao' (dwells on high), which has no basis in the Hebrew and changes the meaning of the verse.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הִנֵּה דוֹר בָּנֶיךָ בָגָדְתִּי' means 'behold, I would have betrayed the generation of Your children' (i.e., the speaker would have been unfaithful to the generation of God's children). The Vietnamese 'thì thật vậy, ta đã phản trọn dòng dõi các con của Ngài' adds 'thật vậy' (truly/surely) which is not in the Hebrew, and 'trọn' (entirely) is an addition not present. More importantly, the Hebrew is a conditional statement ('If I had said... I would have betrayed'), but the Vietnamese renders it as a past completed action ('ta đã phản' = 'I have betrayed'), changing the tense and the hypothetical nature to an actual past event. This changes the meaning: the Hebrew says the speaker would have been guilty of betrayal if he had spoken, not that he actually did betray.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מִקֶּרֶב חוקך' means 'from the midst of your bosom/chest' (i.e., from within Your bosom), but the Vietnamese says 'khỏi lòng Ngài' (from Your heart), which is a different body part. The Hebrew 'חוקך' is 'bosom/chest', not 'heart' (לֵב). This changes the imagery and meaning.; addition: The Vietnamese adds 'kẻ thù' (the enemy) which is not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew 'כַלֵּה' means 'consume/destroy' without specifying the object; the object is implied from context (likely 'them' referring to enemies), but the explicit addition of 'kẻ thù' is an addition not in the Hebrew text.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מָאוֹר וָשָׁמֶשׁ' means 'light and sun' (or 'luminary and sun'), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'mặt trăng và mặt trời' (moon and sun). The word 'מָאוֹר' (ma'or) means 'light' or 'luminary', not specifically 'moon' (which would be 'יָרֵחַ' or 'לְבָנָה'). This changes the meaning by adding 'moon' and dropping 'light'.

name_swap: The Hebrew says 'shepherd of Joseph' (נֹהֵג כַּצֹּאן יוֹסֵף), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'chăn giữ như bầy chiên Gia-cốp' (shepherd like the flock of Jacob), substituting 'Gia-cốp' (Jacob) for 'Y-sô-sép' (Joseph). This is a name swap that changes the referent.

mistranslation: The Hebrew verb עָשַׁנְתָּ (from עָשַׁן, 'to be angry, to smoke/fume') is rendered as 'nổi giận' (to be angry), which is acceptable, but the phrase 'còn nổi giận lời cầu nguyện' is grammatically awkward and could imply anger at the prayer itself. The Hebrew means 'angry against/with the prayer of your people' (i.e., angry at the people because of their prayer, or refusing to hear it). The Vietnamese 'nổi giận lời cầu nguyện' lacks the preposition 'against/with' (against the prayer), making it sound like the anger is directed at the prayer as an object, which is a slight distortion. However, the main issue is that the Hebrew has 'עַד מָתַי' (until when/how long) — the Vietnamese 'cho đến chừng nào' is correct. The verb tense is perfect (עָשַׁנְתָּ) — 'you have been angry' — but Vietnamese uses present 'còn nổi giận' (still angry), which is acceptable contextually. The core meaning is preserved, but the missing preposition changes the object of anger slightly. Given the instruction to flag only substantive differences, this is borderline; however, the phrase 'nổi giận lời cầu nguyện' is a mistranslation because it omits the relational sense (anger against/at the prayer), making it read as if the anger is directed at the prayer itself rather than at the people through their prayer. This is a substantive change in meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְאֹיְבֵינוּ יִלְעֲגוּ לָמוֹ' means 'and our enemies laugh at us' (לָמוֹ = 'at them/us'), but the Vietnamese renders it as 'kẻ thù nghịch chúng tôi thì chế giễu Ngài' ('our enemies mock You'), changing the object from 'us' to 'God'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'שָׂרַי יַחְדָּו מְלָכִים' means 'my princes are kings together' (or 'my officials are all kings'), referring to the speaker's own princes/officials. mistranslation: Hebrew עֲרֵלָה אָזְנָם means 'their ears are uncircumcised' (i.e., closed/blocked), but Vietnamese says 'tai họ bị cắt bì' which means 'their ears are circumcised' — the opposite meaning.

omission: The Hebrew 'אִם יָשׁוּב וְלֹא יָשׁוּב' (if one turns away, will he not return?) is rendered as 'Chúng xây away, vậy mà không trở lại?' — the word 'away' is left in English instead of Vietnamese, and the conditional 'if' (אִם) is omitted, changing the rhetorical question structure.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בַּמָּצוֹר' means 'in the siege' or 'under siege', but the Vietnamese renders it as 'trong thành có vách thành' (in a city with walls), which changes the meaning from a state of siege to a description of a walled city. This is a substantive difference.
